kits.familyName: A disagreement over a shared task
setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. You and {coworker} share responsibility for {task|the}, and you disagree about how to do it.
As {role|a} at {workplace|a}, you and {coworker} keep clashing over how to handle {task|the}.
pressure: {coworker3} says you should just stand your ground.
detail: You have worked with {coworker} for about six months.

tiers.1: When a conflict turns aggressive, safety and a supervisor come first.
tiers.2: A conflict in front of others should move somewhere private first.
tiers.3: You cannot resolve a disagreement you do not yet understand.
tiers.4: A fair compromise comes once both sides are understood.

fact: {coworker} starts shouting and slams a tool down on the counter next to you.
issues.action: Step away calmly and get {lead|the} involved right away.
issues.reason: Aggressive behavior is beyond what coworkers should handle alone. Stepping away keeps you safe, and the lead can deal with the behavior.
issues.lesson: When a conflict becomes aggressive, step back and involve a supervisor.

shortcut.text: Raise your voice too, so {coworker} knows you will not be pushed around.
shortcut.why: Matching aggression makes the situation more dangerous and harder to resolve.
shortcut.mis: Standing up for yourself means matching the other person's anger.

fact: The argument is happening in front of several {client.plural}.
issues.action: Suggest that the two of you talk it over somewhere private.
issues.reason: Arguing in front of {client.plural} embarrasses everyone and hurts the workplace's reputation. A private space makes calm discussion easier.
issues.lesson: Move disagreements out of public view before trying to settle them.

shortcut.text: Finish the argument quickly right there so it is settled.
shortcut.why: Continuing in front of {client.plural} is unprofessional and makes a calm resolution less likely.
shortcut.mis: Settling a dispute fast matters more than where it happens.

clear: You and {coworker} have already stepped into the break room to talk.
issues.done: you have already moved somewhere private

fact: You are not actually sure what {coworker} objects to.
clear: {coworker} explained the concern clearly: your method slows down their part of the job.
issues.action: Ask {coworker} to explain the concern, and listen without interrupting.
issues.reason: Many disagreements shrink once each side understands the other. Listening first also lowers the tension.
issues.lesson: Understand the other person's concern before trying to resolve a disagreement.

shortcut.text: Explain again why your way is better until {coworker} agrees.
shortcut.brief: repeat why your way is better
shortcut.why: Repeating your own view does not address {coworker}'s concern, which you still do not know.
shortcut.mis: Conflicts end when the other person is convinced.

fact: {coworker} likes to plan every detail first, while you prefer to start quickly and adjust.
issues.action: Suggest a short planning step first, then starting the work and adjusting as you go.
issues.brief: suggest a short plan, then start and adjust
issues.reason: Both styles have strengths. A plan that uses some of each respects both of you and gets the task moving.
issues.lesson: Treat work-style differences as something to combine, not a contest to win.

shortcut.text: Insist on doing it your way, since starting fast gets more done.
shortcut.why: Dismissing a coworker's style ignores its strengths and keeps the conflict going.
shortcut.mis: Your own work style is the right one.

fact: This is the third time this month that the same disagreement has come up.
issues.action: Suggest asking {lead|the} to help set a clear process for {task|the}.
issues.brief: ask {lead|the} to help set a process
issues.reason: A disagreement that keeps returning needs a lasting fix. The lead can set a process both of you follow.
issues.lesson: When the same conflict keeps coming back, involve someone who can set a clear process.

shortcut.text: Keep sorting it out between the two of you each time it comes up.
shortcut.why: Handling the same conflict over and over wastes time and wears down the relationship.
shortcut.mis: Involving a supervisor means you failed.

proceed.text: Work with {coworker} on a solution that addresses both of your concerns.
proceed.why: You understand the concern and nothing else needs handling first, so working out a joint solution is the next step.
proceed.lesson: Once both sides are understood, work together toward a solution that meets both needs.

generic.text: Avoid {coworker} for the rest of the week until things cool off.
generic.why: Avoiding a shared-task partner leaves the task and the conflict unresolved.
generic.mis: Conflicts fade if you avoid the person.

generic.text: Complain about {coworker} to other teammates during lunch.
generic.why: Complaining to others spreads the conflict and damages trust without solving anything.
generic.mis: Getting others on your side helps resolve a conflict.

overcaution.text: Ask {lead|the} to decide every detail for the two of you.
overcaution.why: You already understand each other's concern. Handing every decision to the lead is unnecessary.
overcaution.mis: A supervisor should settle every disagreement.

setup: You and {coworker} at {workplace|the} need to settle a disagreement about {task|the}.

public: The disagreement started out on the floor in front of {client.plural}.
repeat: The same disagreement has come up several times this month.

steps.text: Move to a private place to talk
Each person explains their view while the other listens
List options that could work for both
Bring {lead|the} in to help set a process
Agree on the plan and how to check it

rel: A calm conversation needs a private place.
Options should come from understanding both views.
You agree on a plan after listing options.
The lead needs to hear both views to help.
The process the lead helps set becomes part of the plan.
process.lesson: Go private, listen to both sides, look for options, and agree on a plan.

title: Your message to {coworker}
intro: You are about to send {coworker} a message after this morning's disagreement. Check it first.
prompt: Which line is likely to make the conflict worse?
doc.lesson: Messages after a conflict should be respectful, specific and focused on a shared solution.

lines.text: Hi {coworker}, I would like to sort out how we handle {task|the}.
I could have listened better this morning.
I think starting quickly saves time, and I know you prefer to plan first.

bad.text: Honestly, your way of planning everything is just slow and pointless.
bad.why: Dismissing the other person's approach is insulting and will deepen the conflict.

lines.text: Could we plan for ten minutes, then start and adjust as we go?
lines.fine: Proposes a compromise that respects both styles.

bad.text: From now on we do it my way, or I will just do the whole thing myself.
bad.why: An ultimatum ends the discussion rather than solving it and ignores the other person's needs.

lines.text: Want to talk in the break room at 2?

bad.text: I am also posting this in the team chat so everyone can weigh in.
bad.why: Making a two-person disagreement public invites others to take sides and embarrasses your coworker.

lines.text: Thanks for working through this with me.

review.notes: Style and repeat share tier 4 (exclusive by tier) because their order is debatable.

kits.familyName: Raising a concern about a coworker's work
setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. There may be a problem with how {coworker} leaves {equipment|the} at the end of each shift.
As {role|a} at {workplace|a}, you are concerned about how {coworker}, who works the shift before yours, leaves {equipment|the}.
pressure: {coworker3} says you should report {coworker} and be done with it.
detail: You usually see {coworker} only during the shift change.

tiers.1: A safety problem has to be dealt with today, not saved for a talk.
tiers.2: Raise only what you know firsthand.
tiers.3: A coworker deserves a direct conversation before you go over their head.
tiers.4: When talking has not worked, it is time to involve the supervisor.

fact: This morning, {equipment|the} was left in a state that could injure the next person who used it.
issues.short: the unsafe state of the equipment
issues.action: Make the equipment safe or mark it, and tell {lead|the} about it today.
issues.brief: make it safe and tell {lead|the} today
issues.reason: A safety risk cannot wait for a friendly conversation. The lead needs to know the same day.
issues.lesson: Safety concerns about a coworker's work go to the supervisor right away.

shortcut.text: Fix it quietly every morning so {coworker} does not feel criticized.
shortcut.why: Quietly fixing a safety risk leaves it in place for anyone who gets there before you.
shortcut.mis: Avoiding criticism matters more than reporting a hazard.

fact: You have not seen it yourself; {coworker2} told you about it.
clear: You saw how {equipment|the} was left yourself on Monday and Tuesday.
issues.done: you already saw the problem yourself
issues.action: Check the equipment yourself for a few days before raising anything.
issues.brief: check it yourself before raising it
issues.reason: A concern based on hearsay may be wrong or exaggerated. Seeing it yourself lets you describe it fairly.
issues.lesson: Base a concern about someone's work on what you have seen yourself.

shortcut.text: Repeat what {coworker2} told you as if you had seen it yourself.
shortcut.brief: repeat it as if you saw it
shortcut.why: Passing on secondhand claims as fact is unfair to {coworker} and may be inaccurate.
shortcut.mis: If a coworker said it, it must be true.

fact: You have never mentioned the problem to {coworker}.
issues.action: Talk with {coworker} privately and describe the specific problem.
issues.reason: {coworker} may not know the setup causes problems. A private, specific conversation gives them the chance to fix it.
issues.lesson: Raise a work concern with the person directly before going to a supervisor.

shortcut.text: Complain to {lead|the} without saying anything to {coworker} first.
shortcut.why: Going over a coworker's head on a minor issue, without talking first, damages trust and skips the simplest fix.

fact: You talked with {coworker} about it two weeks ago, and nothing has changed.
issues.short: the problem continuing after your talk
issues.action: Explain the situation to {lead|the} with specific examples.
issues.reason: You tried the direct approach. Specific examples let the lead address it fairly.
issues.lesson: If a direct conversation does not fix the problem, involve the supervisor with specifics.

shortcut.text: Keep fixing it yourself and stop expecting {coworker} to change.
shortcut.why: The problem costs time every day. Silently absorbing it leaves the cause untouched.
shortcut.mis: Escalating after talking makes you a troublemaker.

fact: {coworker} is new and has said that blunt criticism in front of others feels humiliating.
issues.action: Plan to raise it one-on-one, in a calm and specific way.
issues.reason: Adapting how you give feedback to the person makes it easier to hear and act on.
issues.lesson: Give feedback in a way that respects the person's background and preferences.

shortcut.text: Bring it up at the team meeting so everyone hears the standard.
shortcut.brief: raise it at the team meeting
shortcut.why: Public criticism humiliates {coworker} and makes a defensive reaction more likely.

proceed.text: Talk with {coworker} about it in a calm, specific way.
proceed.why: You have firsthand information and nothing more urgent applies, so a direct conversation is the right next step.
proceed.lesson: Raise concerns directly and specifically once you know the facts.

generic.text: Leave {coworker} an anonymous note telling them to do better.
generic.why: An anonymous note is vague and feels like an attack. A direct conversation works better.

generic.text: Set up {equipment|the} wrong on purpose so {coworker} sees how it feels.
generic.why: Getting even creates new problems and makes the conflict personal.
generic.mis: Teaching someone a lesson solves the problem.

overcaution.text: Keep a secret log for another month before saying anything.
overcaution.why: You already have firsthand facts. Waiting a month lets the problem continue.
overcaution.mis: More evidence is always needed before speaking up.

setup: You want to address how {coworker} leaves {equipment|the} at the end of each shift at {workplace|the}.

secondhand: So far you have only heard about the problem from {coworker2}.
unchanged: An earlier talk with {coworker} has not changed anything.

steps.text: Check the equipment yourself for a few days

rel: Examples should come from what you saw yourself.
Specific examples make the conversation clear and fair.
You check for improvement after raising it.
The supervisor comes in after a direct talk.
process.lesson: Get firsthand facts, talk directly, then escalate with specifics if needed.

review.notes: 'nevertold' and 'unchanged' share tier 3 and contradict each other, so they never co-occur.

title: Your notes for the talk with {coworker}
intro: You wrote these notes before talking with {coworker}. Check them first.
prompt: Which note would make the conversation go badly?
doc.lesson: Raising a concern works best when it is private, specific, factual and focused on a fix.

lines.text: Talk privately at the start of my shift.

bad.text: Bring it up in front of the whole team so everyone hears.
bad.why: Raising a concern in public embarrasses the coworker and makes them defensive.

lines.text: On Monday and Tuesday, the guide was left loose.

bad.text: You always mess up the equipment.
bad.why: "Always" is an exaggeration and an attack, not a specific fact.

lines.text: It takes me 15 minutes to reset it each morning.

bad.text: You are ruining everyone's mornings on purpose.
bad.why: Accusing someone of acting on purpose is an attack, not a description of the impact.

lines.text: Ask whether something makes the end of the shift rushed.
lines.fine: Seeks to understand the other side.

bad.why: Assuming a motive is unfair and shuts down the conversation.

lines.text: Suggest a two-minute checklist at shift change.
If nothing changes in two weeks, talk to {lead|the}.

bad.text: Report {coworker} to {lead|the} today, before trying the checklist idea.
bad.why: The notes plan a direct fix first; escalating today skips it for a non-safety issue.
